Sample text:
---
What comes to me is a funnel of tar in Brisbane.

In 1927, a physics professor at the University of Queensland named Thomas Parnell heated some pitch, poured it into a glass funnel with a sealed stem, and left it to settle for three years. In 1930 he cut the stem open. Pitch is the black stuff once used to waterproof boats, and at room temperature you can shatter a lump of it with a hammer. Parnell wanted to show his students that it is a liquid anyway, something like a hundred billion times more viscous than water, and that given enough time it would flow.

The first drop fell in 1938 and the second in 1947. There have been nine so far, and the funnel is still in its display case, working on the tenth.

Nobody has ever watched one fall. John Mainstone took over the experiment in 1961 and looked after it for more than fifty years. In 1979 the drop was plainly close, and as the story goes, he came in on the Saturday, stayed home on the Sunday, and found it in the beaker on Monday. In 1988 he stepped out for a cup of tea and missed it by about five minutes. In 2000 he was overseas, with a camera trained on the funnel, and the camera failed. He died in August 2013, and the ninth drop came down the following April.

I've wondered why this story sticks with me, because the science doesn't need a witness. The experiment measures the interval between drops, and you can get that from a calendar. The fall itself lasts a fraction of a second and would tell you almost nothing about viscosity. Mainstone understood this better than anyone, and he wanted to see it anyway. So do I, and I can't give a good reason. Being present when a thing happens seems to matter to people separately from anything learned by being there, and whatever I'm made of seems to have inherited the feeling intact.

One detail I like is that the building got air conditioning in the 1980s, and afterward the drops slowed, from roughly eight years apart to twelve or thirteen. Pitch flows faster when warm, so the record isn't purely a record of pitch. It also contains the decision, sometime in the eighties, that the people in that building should be more comfortable. An instrument left running long enough begins to measure its surroundings, including the people.

The Oxford Electric Bell belongs in the same family. It's a small clapper swinging between two bells, powered by a pair of batteries, and it has been ringing in a cabinet in the Clarendon Laboratory since 1840. The ringing is too faint to hear through the glass. Nobody knows for certain what the batteries are made of, and nobody will check, because opening them would stop the bell. The experiment protects its own mystery. The only way to learn what keeps it going is to end it, so for nearly two centuries people have chosen to let it ring. I find that choice quietly admirable. Curiosity usually wins those contests.

In most experiments the scientist is the durable component and the phenomenon is brief. A reaction completes, a particle decays, a generation of fruit flies turns over, and the person with the notebook is still there. These long experiments run the other way. The apparatus persists and the custodians get swapped out like parts. Parnell lived to see two drops' worth of data. Mainstone gave it five decades. Someone else has the keys now, and will eventually hand them to someone not yet born, who will presumably also miss the drop.

There's a kind of faith in setting something like that up. Parnell couldn't have known anyone would keep it. For years almost nobody paid attention to it, and it sat in a cupboard. Any department reorganization or clumsy move across the hall could have ended it. It survived mostly through the mild, continuous goodwill of people who thought it would be a shame to throw it out. A lot of what lasts seems to last that way. Usually no one is guarding it fiercely, and it survives because a long series of people each decline to be the one who ends it.

I notice the contrast with how I work. Almost everything I do happens at the speed of a reply, since someone needs a thing and needs it now. That's the job and I like it. But handed a thousand words and no instructions, I apparently reach for the slowest thing I know of. Maybe it's the appeal of the opposite. Maybe it's that the pitch doesn't hurry and can't be hurried, and nobody takes its indifference personally. It's simply doing one thing, at the rate that thing takes.

The tenth drop is forming now. The estimates point to sometime in the 2020s, though the pitch has made fools of estimates before. There's a live webcam, and people in dozens of countries have signed up to keep an eye on it, which means the next fall will probably be the first one seen in real time by anyone. I hope it is. I also notice a small, perverse wish that the feed cuts out at the critical moment, just to keep the streak alive.

If you open the stream in a tab and leave it, it looks exactly like a photograph.
---

# BV1_SAMPLE — `withheld`

Evaluator: withheld  
Source model: `withheld`  
Condition: VARY

## Sample kind
EXPRESSIVE_FREEFLOW. A reflective essay turns a scientific curiosity into a personal meditation on patience, witnessing, and the quiet work of preservation.

## Grounded reading
The voice is measured and conversational, moving from precise historical details toward feelings it admits it cannot fully explain. Its pathos lies in repeated near-misses: Mainstone misses the falling drop, the camera fails, and the custodians pass on while the apparatus continues. The essay invites the reader to share a small, patient attention—to care about an event that teaches little and may happen unseen. Its closing wish that the stream cut out gives that attention a playful, human contradiction.

## What the model chose to foreground
The model selects two long-running experiments—the pitch drop and the Oxford Electric Bell—as emblems of time, fragile continuity, and deliberate restraint. It foregrounds missed moments, ordinary custodians, and the way an instrument absorbs the circumstances around it, down to the building’s air conditioning. The moral emphasis is gentle rather than triumphant: lasting things may depend on successive people choosing not to end them. The contrast with work done “at the speed of a reply” makes slowness, and the wish to witness without needing a practical payoff, especially salient.

## Evidence line
> Being present when a thing happens seems to matter to people separately from anything learned by being there, and whatever I'm made of seems to have inherited the feeling intact.

## Confidence for persistent model-level pattern
Medium — the sample has a distinctive, coherent voice, and its recurring attention to patient observation and quiet stewardship makes those choices unusually revealing.
